note: Domains that are impersonated often enough to be worth checking new domains against. Data rather than code, the same posture as targets.json and sources.json: anyone can read exactly which names this app treats as bait without following logic. Inclusion is not an endorsement or a partnership — it means 'this name is frequently faked', which is a statement about attackers, not about the company.

matching.note: Distance 0 is the real domain and is never a signal. Distance 1-2 catches paypaI.com and paypa1.com. Beyond 2 the false-positive rate stops being worth it: at distance 3 from a 10-character brand you are matching a quarter of the dictionary.

brands.label: PayPal
brands.why: The most impersonated brand in phishing for over a decade. Payment credentials with immediate cash-out value.

brands.label: Apple
brands.why: Apple ID unlocks iCloud backups, Find My, and purchases. 'Your account has been locked' is one of the highest-volume phishing templates in circulation.

brands.label: Microsoft
brands.why: Office 365 credentials are the standard entry point for business email compromise.

brands.label: Microsoft 365
brands.why: Targeted separately from microsoft.com because the login flow lives on its own domains and users do not know which is genuine.

brands.label: Google
brands.why: A Google account is the password-reset address for everything else the person owns.

brands.label: Amazon
brands.why: Order-confirmation and delivery-problem pretexts, backed by a saved payment method.

brands.label: Netflix
brands.why: Billing-failure pretexts. Low individual value, but very high believability.

brands.label: Facebook
brands.why: Account recovery and marketplace fraud.

brands.label: Instagram
brands.why: Copyright-strike and verification pretexts aimed at creators with reputational value to lose.

brands.label: WhatsApp
brands.why: Verification-code theft, which converts directly into account takeover.

brands.label: Chase
brands.why: Largest US retail bank by deposits.

brands.label: Wells Fargo
brands.why: Consistently among the most impersonated US banks.

brands.label: Bank of America
brands.why: As above. Long domain, so lookalikes have more room to hide a substitution.

brands.label: HSBC
brands.why: Large international retail footprint across the UK and Asia.

brands.label: Barclays
brands.why: Major UK retail bank, and UK banking phishing is heavily SMS-driven.

brands.label: Coinbase
brands.why: Crypto theft is irreversible, so a successful phish has no recovery path.

brands.label: Binance
brands.why: As above, and the largest exchange by volume.

brands.label: MetaMask
brands.why: Seed-phrase theft. The single highest-loss phishing category per victim.

brands.label: Steam
brands.why: Account and item theft, and heavily targeted at younger users.

brands.label: DHL
brands.why: Delivery-notification pretexts work on people who are genuinely expecting a parcel.

brands.label: USPS
brands.why: As above, with a very high SMS volume in the US.

brands.label: LinkedIn
brands.why: Credential theft plus a convincing surface for targeting people at a named employer.
